questions.q: What is the literal meaning of the phrase "a sordid boon" in line 4, and which two words create the oxymoron?
questions.a: "A sordid boon" means a base or morally degraded gift; the oxymoron is formed by "sordid" (ignoble, dirty) and "boon" (blessing, benefit). A wrong answer that misses the oxymoron shows the student is reading for plot only, not for the tension between words that signals a secondary theme of corrupted spirituality.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why the speaker says "We have given our hearts away" (line 4) and connect it to the secondary theme of spiritual alienation.
questions.a: The speaker means humans have traded their capacity for wonder and emotional connection to nature for material gain; this transaction creates spiritual alienation because the heart — the organ of feeling — is no longer attuned to the natural world. A wrong answer that treats "hearts" as merely "love" or "feelings" without linking to the transactional language ("given away") misses the economic metaphor that drives the secondary theme of commodification of the self.

questions.q: Identify two images from the octave (first eight lines) that personify nature as vulnerable or suppressed, and explain how each supports the secondary theme of nature's muted power.
questions.a: 1) "The Sea that bares her bosom to the moon" — the sea is a woman exposing herself, suggesting openness and vulnerability. 2) "The Winds that will be howling at all hours, / And are up-gathered now like sleeping flowers" — the winds are powerful but currently stilled, like flowers gathered in a bunch. Both images show nature's energy contained or ignored, reinforcing the theme that nature's power exists but is unheeded by humanity. A wrong answer that lists images without explaining the "muted" quality fails to analyze how personification serves the theme.

questions.q: Compare the speaker's attitude toward "civilised society" and "a Pagan creed outworn" in the sestet. What does this comparison reveal about the secondary theme of historical nostalgia as critique?
questions.a: The speaker rejects modern civilisation as "out of tune" and prefers an "outworn" Pagan creed because it offered direct sensory communion with nature (Proteus, Triton). This reveals that the secondary theme is not mere escapism but a radical critique: the "outworn" past is valued precisely because it kept humanity in tune with nature, whereas "civilised" modernity has severed that bond. A wrong answer that calls the Pagan wish "simple escapism" misses the satirical force — the speaker uses an allegedly backward belief to judge the forward march of progress.

questions.q: Evaluate the effectiveness of the mythological allusions (Proteus, Triton) in the final two lines. Do they strengthen or weaken the poem's argument about reconnecting with nature? Justify.
questions.a: They strengthen the argument by making the alternative concrete: Proteus (shape-shifting truth) and Triton (announcing presence) represent a nature that is alive, communicative, and responsive — exactly what the modern world lacks. The allusions are not decorative; they function as proof that a different relationship with nature once existed in human imagination. A wrong answer that dismisses them as "just Greek myths" fails to see that the poem itself argues for the power of myth to re-enchant the world.

questions.q: Write a four-line stanza in the style of Wordsworth that introduces a new secondary theme: the role of technology (e.g., smartphones) as the modern equivalent of "getting and spending". Use at least one personification and one contrast.
questions.a: Example: "The screen that glows in midnight's quiet room, / Steals dawn's first light and binds the waking mind; / We scroll for lives not ours, and call it boom, / While real birds sing, unheard, by us confined." A poor answer that merely describes phones without personification or contrast shows the student cannot transfer the poem's technique to a new context, indicating surface-level understanding.
